Defines the limited jurisdiction of the Industrial Tribunal to grant approval for dismissal, requiring only a prima facie case rather than a full re-appreciation of evidence.
The court considered whether Section 4, which prohibits suits to recover benami property, applied retrospectively to suits filed before the Act came into force.

rules.case_name: R. Rajagopal Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan
rules.reference: R. Rajagopal Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to hold that Section 4 of the Benami Act is prospective and does not bar suits filed prior to the Act's commencement.

rules.case_name: Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare
rules.reference: Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare
rules.relevance: The court noted that this earlier judgment, which held the Act to be retroactive, was overruled by R. Rajagopal Reddy.
The court used this section to support the inference that a notice sent by postal certificate was duly served in the normal course of business.
The court referred to this section regarding the relevance of the course of business in determining if a letter was dispatched and received.

rules.case_name: Harihar Banerji v. Ramshashi Roy
rules.relevance: The court relied on this Privy Council judgment for the principle that a properly directed letter put into the post is presumed to have reached its destination.

rules.case_name: Ganga Ram v. Smt. Phulwati
rules.relevance: The court referred to this judgment to support the presumption that letters delivered to the post office are duly delivered to the addressee in the normal course.

rules.case_name: Mst. L.M.S. Ummu Saleema v. S.S. Gujarat
rules.reference: Mst. L.M.S. Ummu Saleema v. S.S. Gujarat
rules.relevance: The court referred to this case to establish that the presumption of service from a postal certificate is permissible but not inevitable and can be rebutted.
Establishes that when terms of a contract are reduced to writing, no evidence other than the document itself can be admitted to prove those terms.

The court held that an agreement without consideration is not void if it is in writing, registered, and made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation, such as brothers.
Defines the offence of dishonor of cheque and imposes conditions precedent, including the requirement to issue a demand notice within thirty days of receipt of intimation of dishonor.
Defines the power to grant anticipatory bail as an extraordinary remedy to be exercised only in exceptional cases where there is a genuine apprehension of arrest.
Provides for the issuance of proclamation against a person absconding; the court held that a person declared a proclaimed offender under this section is not entitled to anticipatory bail.

rules.case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Pradeep Sharma
rules.reference: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Pradeep Sharma
rules.relevance: Established the principle that a person declared as an absconder or proclaimed offender under Section 82 Cr.P.C. is not entitled to the relief of anticipatory bail.
Provides for attachment of property of a proclaimed offender; proceedings under this section reinforce the finding that the accused was absconding.

rules.case_name: Lavesh v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Cited in Pradeep Sharma to reiterate that when an accused is absconding and declared a proclaimed offender, there is no question of granting anticipatory bail.

The court held that the mere fact that an accusation arises out of a business transaction does not automatically entitle the accused to anticipatory bail if serious offences like cheating are alleged.
Empowers the court to pass any order necessary for doing complete justice, used here to direct that the settlement amount need not be refunded.
Establishes that liberty cannot be taken away except by procedure established by law, rendering principles of estoppel or waiver inapplicable to cure procedural defects in criminal convictions.
Used to interpret the calculation of time periods, distinguishing between 'from' and 'within' to determine if the 30-day period was strictly adhered to.
Defines criminal breach of trust by a public servant, requiring that property be 'entrusted' to the accused.
Prohibits public servants from accepting gratification other than legal remuneration, requiring entrustment of property.
The court affirmed the High Court's view that the Act is inapplicable to offences punishable with life imprisonment (Section 409 IPC) and offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act.

rules.case_name: The State v. Dahyalal Dalpatram
rules.relevance: Disapproved the view that money collected by a public servant in excess of what is due is not entrusted; held that a public servant collecting money is entrusted with it even if the liability was not legally enforceable.

rules.case_name: Surendra Pal Singh v. The State
rules.reference: Surendra Pal Singh v. The State
rules.relevance: Appellant relied on this case to argue money collected by cheating is not entrusted. The court noted it was disapproved by Dahyalal Dalpatram.

rules.case_name: In re: Ramappa
rules.relevance: Established that receiving money as a servant for a specific purpose constitutes entrustment, even if obtained by false pretences, making subsequent misappropriation criminal breach of trust.

rules.case_name: The Crown Prosecutor v. J. McIver and K. S. Narasimhachari
rules.reference: The Crown Prosecutor v. J. McIver and K. S. Narasimhachari
rules.relevance: Confirmed that the completion of the offence of cheating upon receipt of property does not preclude a charge of criminal breach of trust for subsequent misappropriation.

The court applied this section to determine the essential ingredients of the offence, specifically the requirement that gratification must be received as a motive or reward for inducing a public servant to do or forbear from doing an official act.
Requires prior sanction for prosecution of public servants; the validity of this sanction was the central issue.
Cited in the context of provisions relating to alleged defects in sanction.
The court considered whether the resolution violated the requirement that only registered practitioners with recognized qualifications could hold government office.
The court relied on this provision to determine that rights conferred on registered practitioners were preserved and not affected by Section 15(2).
The court examined this section in conjunction with the Central Act to determine the legality of the promotion criteria.
The court noted that recruitment and conditions of service for teaching posts are governed by rules framed under this article.

rules.reference: Orissa Homeopathic Medical Teaching Service (Method of Recruitment and Conditions of Service) Rules, 1980
rules.relevance: The court used these rules to establish that college teachers belong to a separate cadre from peripheral medical officers.

rules.case_name: State of Orissa and another v. Radheshyam Nanda
rules.reference: State of Orissa and another v. Radheshyam Nanda
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent for the interpretation of Sections 15(2) and 15(3) of the Central Act and Section 29(b) of the 1956 Act.

rules.reference: Separate cadres cannot be treated as discriminatory for promotion purposes
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that excluding one cadre (teachers) from a post reserved for another cadre (peripheral officers) is not discriminatory if the cadres are distinct.
Guarantees equal opportunity in public employment; reservation cannot efface this guarantee.
Allows special provisions for backward classes but is an exception to Article 16(1) and must not create a monopoly or render equality illusory.
Defines 'cadre' as the strength of a service or part of a service sanctioned as a separate unit.

rules.case_name: Samar Ghosh v. Jaya Ghosh
rules.relevance: Defines mental cruelty as a concept that cannot be defined by a straitjacket formula and must be evaluated based on peculiar facts and circumstances.
Governs the admissibility of secondary evidence when the original document is not produced.

rules.case_name: Ashok Dulichand v. Madhavlal Dube
rules.relevance: Establishes that secondary evidence is admissible only if a proper foundation is laid showing the original is in the possession of the person against whom it is sought to be proved.

rules.case_name: H. Siddiqui (Dead) by Lrs. v. A. Ramalingam
rules.reference: H. Siddiqui (Dead) by Lrs. v. A. Ramalingam
rules.relevance: Holds that secondary evidence is inadmissible if no factual foundation is laid for the non-production of the original document.

rules.case_name: Vishwanath Agrawal v. Sara Vishwanath Agrawal
rules.reference: Vishwanath Agrawal v. Sara Vishwanath Agrawal
rules.relevance: Establishes that a sustained attitude of causing humiliation and calculated torture amounts to mental cruelty.
Defines the scope of the Supreme Court's special leave jurisdiction, particularly regarding interference with concurrent findings of fact.
A specific case for desertion must be pleaded in the petition for divorce; a finding cannot be sustained on an unpleaded ground.

rules.case_name: Vinny Parmvir Parmar v. Parmvir Parmar
rules.reference: Vinny Parmvir Parmar v. Parmvir Parmar
rules.relevance: Guides the determination of permanent alimony based on the wife's status, mode of life, and the husband's financial capacity.
Empowers the Supreme Court to pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it.
Defines cruelty as a ground for divorce. The court considered this ground despite it not being explicitly pleaded in the relief clause.

The court considered this provision to determine that once an enquiry is held legal, the only question for the adjudicating authority is whether the punishment is disproportionate to the gravity of the charge.

rules.case_name: The Workmen of Mis Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co. of India (Pvt.) Ltd. vs. The Management & Ors.
rules.reference: The Workmen of Mis Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co. of India (Pvt.) Ltd. vs. The Management & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent for the principle that the court must examine if the punishment imposed is disproportionate to the gravity of the charge.

rules.case_name: Divisional Controller, Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation vs. M.G. Vittal Rao
rules.reference: Divisional Controller, Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation vs. M.G. Vittal Rao
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to establish that acquittal in criminal court does not vitiate a departmental enquiry because the standard of proof differs (preponderance of probabilities vs. beyond reasonable doubt).

rules.case_name: Shankar Chakravarti vs. Britannia Biscuits Co. Ltd. & Anr.
rules.reference: Shankar Chakravarti vs. Britannia Biscuits Co. Ltd. & Anr.
rules.relevance: The court referred to this case to distinguish the current situation, noting that remand for fresh evidence is only necessary if the enquiry is found illegal, which was not the case here.

rules.reference: Standard of proof in domestic enquiry vs. criminal trial
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that domestic enquiries require proof on preponderance of probabilities, whereas criminal cases require proof beyond reasonable doubt, allowing independent findings.

rules.reference: Independence of departmental proceedings from criminal proceedings
rules.relevance: The court held that departmental proceedings are separate from criminal proceedings and an employer has the right to conduct an enquiry independently of the outcome of a criminal case.

rules.reference: Indian Railway Construction Co. Ltd. (Conduct, Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1981
rules.relevance: Governs the special procedure allowing a disciplinary authority to dispense with an enquiry if satisfied that it is not reasonably practicable to hold one, provided reasons are recorded in writing.

The court considered whether the protection against dismissal without enquiry applied, ultimately noting the Division Bench held it was not attracted, and focusing instead on the statutory rules and judicial review principles.

rules.case_name: Council of Civil Service Unions v. Minister for the Civil Service
rules.reference: Council of Civil Service Unions v. Minister for the Civil Service
rules.relevance: Established the grounds for judicial review of administrative action: illegality, irrationality, and procedural impropriety.

rules.case_name: Associated Provincial Picture Houses v. Wednesbury Corpn.
rules.reference: Associated Provincial Picture Houses v. Wednesbury Corpn.
rules.relevance: Defined 'Wednesbury unreasonableness', stating that a decision is unreasonable if no sensible person could have arrived at it, limiting judicial interference in administrative discretion.

rules.reference: U.P. State Electricity Board (Employees' Retirement) Regulations, 1975
rules.relevance: The court relied on this regulation to establish that the retirement age is fixed at 58 years, with retention beyond that age requiring specific written sanction from the Board, distinguishing it from uncontrolled management discretion.

rules.case_name: Hindustan Antibiotics Ltd. v. The Workmen
rules.reference: Hindustan Antibiotics Ltd. v. The Workmen
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this precedent because it involved a rule granting uncontrolled discretion to management to extend retirement age from 55 to 60, whereas the present case involves a specific regulatory framework fixing the age at 58 with strict conditions for extension.
The court noted that this provision was raised but not argued before the High Court, and therefore the High Court was not called upon to decide the issue.
These articles vest the power of dismissal, removal, or termination of District Judges in the Governor, limiting the High Court to a recommending role.
Rule 14 defines the age of superannuation as 60 years and does not provide for retrospective retirement at an earlier age.

rules.case_name: Registrar (Admn.), High Court of Orissa, Cuttack vs. Sisir Kanta Satapathy (Dead) by LRs. and Anr.
rules.reference: Registrar (Admn.), High Court of Orissa, Cuttack vs. Sisir Kanta Satapathy (Dead) by LRs. and Anr.
rules.relevance: Established that the High Court cannot dismiss or remove judicial officers; it can only recommend such action to the Governor.
Establishes the Government's power to regulate conditions of service, including the age of retirement.
The court considered whether the reduction in retirement age amounted to 'removal' requiring the procedural safeguards of Article 311(2).

rules.case_name: Moti Ram Deka v. General Manager, North Frontier Railway
rules.reference: Moti Ram Deka v. General Manager, North Frontier Railway
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case, noting it dealt with termination by notice rather than superannuation, and relied on its holding that retirement due to age does not amount to removal under Article 311.

The specific offences alleged in the FIR and charge-sheet, namely cheating, criminal breach of trust, and common intention.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana and Others Vs. Bhajan Lal and Others
rules.reference: State of Haryana and Others Vs. Bhajan Lal and Others
rules.relevance: Establishes the categories of cases where inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC can be exercised, emphasizing that such power is extraordinary and must be used with circumspection.

rules.case_name: Trisuns Chemical Industry Vs. Rajesh Agarwal and Ors.
rules.reference: Trisuns Chemical Industry Vs. Rajesh Agarwal and Ors.
rules.relevance: Holds that the existence of an arbitration clause or civil remedy does not preclude criminal prosecution for offences like cheating, as arbitration cannot try criminal acts.

rules.case_name: Nagpur Steel & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. Vs. P. Radhakrishna and Others
rules.reference: Nagpur Steel & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. Vs. P. Radhakrishna and Others
rules.relevance: Establishes that a complaint in a commercial transaction warrants trial if it discloses an offence, and the truth of allegations is to be determined at trial.

The court discussed the High Court's discretionary jurisdiction to quash proceedings, noting it should not be exercised to quash cases involving crimes against society where a prima facie case exists.
This section lists compoundable offences. The court considered whether the restriction on compounding under this section limits the High Court's power under Section 482.

rules.case_name: Gian Singh vs. State of Punjab and Another
rules.reference: Gian Singh vs. State of Punjab and Another
rules.relevance: Established that the power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is distinct from the power to compound offences under Section 320 Cr.P.C., but the High Court must consider the nature and gravity of the offence. The court distinguished the specific observation regarding the Prevention of Corruption Act in this case.
One of the offences charged against the respondents; it is a compoundable offence.

Empowers High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose. The scope of this power against private bodies was central to the dispute.

rules.case_name: Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi
rules.reference: Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi
rules.relevance: Laid down six tests to determine if a body is an instrumentality or agency of the State, including shareholding, financial assistance, monopoly status, deep and pervasive State control, public importance of functions, and transfer of government departments.

rules.case_name: Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology
rules.reference: Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology
rules.relevance: Clarified that the tests in Ajay Hasia are not rigid and that regulatory control does not equate to pervasive State control. A body is 'State' only if it is financially, functionally, and administratively dominated by or under the control of the Government.

rules.case_name: U.P. State Co-operative Land Development Bank Ltd. v. Chandra Bhan Dubey
rules.reference: U.P. State Co-operative Land Development Bank Ltd. v. Chandra Bhan Dubey
rules.relevance: The High Court relied on this case, but the Supreme Court distinguished it, noting that the U.P. Land Development Bank had pervasive State control, statutory service rules, and State guarantees, unlike the private Federal Bank.

rules.reference: Andi Mukta Sadguru Shree Muktajee Vandas Swami Suvarna Jayanti Mahotsav Smarak Trust v. V.R. Rudani

Referenced to demonstrate that regulatory controls exist for all companies, not just banks, and do not make them State instrumentalities.
Writ jurisdiction in contract matters is limited to cases where state action is arbitrary, unfair, or unreasonable; it does not extend to resolving serious disputed questions of fact.

rules.case_name: M/s Hyderabad Commercials v. Indian Bank
rules.reference: M/s Hyderabad Commercials v. Indian Bank
rules.relevance: Distinguished because liability was admitted in that case, whereas here fraud and depositor involvement are disputed and under criminal investigation.

rules.reference: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013

rules.case_name: Indore Development Authority v. Manoharlal and Others

rules.relevance: A party cannot take advantage of a situation created by their own wrong, such as obtaining interim stays to delay possession.
The law does not expect the performance of the impossible; the authority could not take possession while a stay was in effect.
Empowers the Supreme Court to pass any order necessary for doing complete justice between the parties.

rules.case_name: Jaipur Development Authority v. Mahesh Sharma and Another

Findings of fact by an arbitral tribunal are not subject to appellate scrutiny unless they are perverse or based on no evidence.
A fundamental breach allows the innocent party to terminate the contract and claim damages for the entire contract, including unperformed parts.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Sugauli Sugar Works (P) Ltd.

rules.case_name: McDermott International Inc. v. Burn Standard Co. Ltd.

rules.case_name: Juggilal Kamlal Jinnah v. Pratapmal Rameshwar

rules.case_name: Suisse Atlantique Societe d’Armament SA v. NV Rotterdamsche Kolen Centrale

rules.reference: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002

An appellate court should not interfere with trial court findings without indicating reasons or analyzing the evidence; unreasoned judgments disclosing non-application of mind are liable to be set aside.

rules.reference: Disciplinary action based on decision-making process, not outcome

rules.reference: Misconduct requires proof of extraneous considerations or illegal gratification
rules.relevance: The court held that mere suspicion or erroneous outcomes do not constitute misconduct; there must be evidence of illegal gratification or extraneous considerations vitiating the process.
The charges against the appellant alleged misconduct within the meaning of this rule due to alleged extraneous considerations in judicial decisions.
Prohibits courts from taking cognizance of offences against public justice except on the complaint of the court in which the offence was committed or a court to which it is subordinate.
Defines 'subordinate' for the purposes of Section 195(1)(b) as the court to which appeals 'ordinarily' lie from the former court.
Prescribes the procedure for making complaints under Section 195, allowing a subordinate court to exercise the power if the original court has not done so.
Applies the Code of Civil Procedure to proceedings under the Act, subject to inconsistencies, but does not override the specific appellate structure of the Act.
Defines subordination of courts for the purposes of the CPC, which the court distinguished from the subordination required under Section 195 Cr.P.C.
Defines the punishment for voluntarily causing grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means, including corrosive substances like acid.

Referenced to highlight the legislative recognition of the gravity of acid attacks, though not applicable to the 1997 offence.
The Supreme Court will not interfere with concurrent findings of fact by subordinate courts unless such findings are perverse or infirm.

The court applied Section 34 to establish joint liability, noting that common intention can be inferred from circumstances and does not require identical acts or personal infliction of injury by every accused.
The court considered the principle that appellate courts should not interfere with sentencing unless there are compelling reasons, particularly in heinous crimes where deterrence is necessary.

The court analyzed Section 307 to determine if the act was done with the intention or knowledge that, if death resulted, it would constitute murder, noting that the nature of the injury helps deduce intent.
The substantive law under which the appellants were charged and convicted for murder.

rules.case_name: Ashok Kumar v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Ashok Kumar v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Cited to support the principle that common intention is the essential element for Section 34 and that acts of participants need not be identical.
The principle that accused persons are entitled to the benefit of doubt when the prosecution fails to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to weak or suppressed evidence.
Empowers the State Legislature to adopt any one or more languages in use in the State, or Hindi, for official purposes. The court interpreted this to allow multiple adoptions from time to time.

Applies the General Clauses Act, 1897, to the interpretation of the Constitution.

The impugned legislation declaring Urdu as a second official language, upheld as constitutional.
Guarantees minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions, which the court interpreted as subject to reasonable state regulations.
Protects the right of any section of citizens to conserve their distinctive language, script, or culture.
Prohibits denial of admission to educational institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste, or language, balancing minority rights with individual citizen rights.

rules.case_name: Rev. Sidhajbhai Sabhai v. State of Bombay
rules.reference: Rev. Sidhajbhai Sabhai v. State of Bombay
rules.relevance: Established that reasonable regulations in the interest of efficiency, discipline, and public order can be imposed on minority institutions without violating Article 30.

rules.case_name: TMA Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka

rules.relevance: Held that the right under Article 30 is not absolute and must yield to regulations framed in the national interest and for the welfare of students.

rules.reference: Correction of date of birth at the fag end of service
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that requests for correction of date of birth in service records are generally not sustainable at the fag end of service to prevent adverse effects on junior employees' promotions and to discourage belated claims.

rules.case_name: Home Deptt. v. R. Kirubakaran
rules.relevance: Held that correction at the fag end causes a chain reaction affecting promotions of junior employees and requires conclusive proof of real injustice.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra and Anr. vs. Gorakhnath Sitaram Kamble & Ors.
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra and Anr. vs. Gorakhnath Sitaram Kamble & Ors.

rules.case_name: State of M.P. vs. Premlal Shrivas
rules.reference: State of M.P. vs. Premlal Shrivas
rules.relevance: Held that even with good evidence, correction cannot be claimed as a matter of right if the application is filed after a long lapse of time, and courts cannot aid those who sleep over their rights.

rules.case_name: M/s Eastern Coalfields Ltd. & Ors. vs. Ram Samugh Yadav & Ors.

rules.relevance: Held that raising a dispute regarding date of birth only one year prior to superannuation, without earlier objection, is a belated dispute.

rules.reference: Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. & Ors. vs. Chhota Birasa Uranw

rules.case_name: Union of India v. C. Rama Swamy

Governs the condonation of delay in filing appeals, requiring the appellant to show 'sufficient cause' for the delay.

rules.case_name: Ramlal, Motilal and Chhotelal Vs. Rewa Coalfields Ltd.

rules.case_name: P.K. Ramachandran Vs. State of Kerala and Anr.
rules.reference: P.K. Ramachandran Vs. State of Kerala and Anr.

rules.case_name: Pundlik Jalam Patil Vs. Executive Engineer, Jalgaon Medium Project

rules.relevance: Reinforces that laws of limitation are based on public policy to ensure an end to litigation and that courts assist the vigilant, not those who slumber over their rights.

rules.reference: Basawaraj and Anr. Vs. Special Land Acquisition Officer
rules.relevance: Holds that 'sufficient cause' cannot be liberally interpreted if negligence, inaction, or lack of bona fides is attributed to the party, and condoning delay without sufficient cause violates statutory principles.

rules.case_name: State of M.P. and another vs. Pradeep Kumar and another
rules.reference: State of M.P. and another vs. Pradeep Kumar and another
rules.relevance: Held that failure to file a condonation application simultaneously with the appeal is not fatal and the defect can be cured.

rules.case_name: Smt. Fuljit Kaur Vs. State of Punjab & Ors.

rules.relevance: The Court relied on the reasons recorded in this parallel judgment to determine the validity of the High Court's order in the present appeal.

rules.case_name: Esha Bhattacharjee vs. Managing Committee of Raghunathpur Nafar Academy
rules.reference: Esha Bhattacharjee vs. Managing Committee of Raghunathpur Nafar Academy

rules.relevance: Establishes that allegations of excessive or retaliatory force resulting in death necessitate a thorough enquiry.

rules.case_name: Bharati Tanning v. Union of India & Ors

rules.relevance: Supports the constitution of a Special Investigating Team to ensure criminal prosecution is carried on without deficiency.

rules.case_name: R.S. Sodhi v. State of U.P.

rules.case_name: State of West Bengal and Ors. Vs. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights, West Bengal and Ors.

Stipulates that the widow and minor children of a temporary Railway servant who dies while in service after not less than one year of continuous qualifying service are eligible for family pension.
Governs the grant of family pension to the dependents of deceased temporary servants.

The Supreme Court generally does not interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts unless there is a perversity or misapplication of law.

Limits the relief the NGT can grant to compensation, restitution of property, or restitution of the environment.

rules.case_name: Sukhendu Das v. Rita Mukherjee

rules.case_name: Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan

rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to establish that waiver requires conscious abandonment of rights and that mere acts of indulgence or inconsistent conduct without reliance by the other party do not amount to waiver.

rules.reference: Waiver of rights requires conscious abandonment
rules.relevance: The court applied this principle to determine that the respondent's conduct did not constitute a waiver of his statutory right to pension.

rules.reference: Employees Provident Fund and Family Pension Fund Act, 1952
rules.relevance: Provides the statutory basis for the Employees Family Pension Scheme, 1971.
Mandates that employees must exercise an option to avail of family pension benefits within a specified period; failure to opt results in entitlement to Provident Fund benefits instead.
The Supreme Court may interfere with concurrent findings of fact only if they are perverse or based on a misappreciation of evidence.
The court examined whether the classification of employees based on the date of absorption was arbitrary and lacked a rational nexus with the object of the legislation.

The court relied on this rule to establish that family pension is granted specifically to the widow/widower and minor children, and does not provide for nomination or payment to other relatives like a brother.

rules.case_name: Jodh Singh v. Union of India & Anr.
rules.reference: Jodh Singh v. Union of India & Anr.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to establish that family pension is admissible on account of the status of a widow and does not form part of the deceased's estate, thus cannot be disposed of by will.

rules.reference: Reserve Bank of India Guidelines for compromise settlement of chronic Non-Performing Assets (NPAs)
rules.relevance: The court analyzed these guidelines to determine that they were internal executive instructions without statutory force and did not create a legal right for borrowers. The guidelines specifically required accounts to be classified as NPA (sub-standard, doubtful, or loss) as on March 31, 2000, to be eligible.

rules.reference: Writ of Mandamus requires a statutory duty and legal right
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that mandamus can only be issued to enforce a plain, positive, specific, and ministerial duty imposed by law or statute. It cannot be used to enforce contractual obligations or internal guidelines where no statutory duty exists.

rules.case_name: Bihar Eastern Gangetic Fishermen Cooperative Society Ltd. v. Sipahi Singh
rules.reference: Bihar Eastern Gangetic Fishermen Cooperative Society Ltd. v. Sipahi Singh
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to establish that a writ of mandamus cannot be granted to enforce an obligation flowing from a contract or where no statute imposes a legal duty on the authority.

rules.reference: Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993
rules.relevance: The court held that the respondents had a statutory remedy to appeal the DRT decree under this section. By failing to exercise this remedy, the decree attained finality, and the High Court could not bypass this statutory process via a writ petition.

rules.reference: Consent of counsel does not bind client without instructions
rules.relevance: The court rejected the argument that the order was passed on consent, holding that a counsel's statement that the client would 'consider' a proposal does not amount to binding consent.
Empowers the RBI to issue directions to banking companies in the interest of banking policy.
Empowers the RBI to determine policy regarding advances and mandates that banking companies are bound to comply with such directions.
Prohibits arbitrary state action and ensures equality; the court held that discriminatory deviation from RBI guidelines violates this article.
Defines 'State' to include public sector banks, making them subject to fundamental rights obligations.
Mandates that the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within India, requiring adherence to Constitution Bench judgments.
Governs the power of the High Court to grant bail and the standards for exercising such discretion.

rules.case_name: Ram Govind Upadhyay v. Sudarshan Singh and Others
rules.reference: Ram Govind Upadhyay v. Sudarshan Singh and Others
rules.relevance: Establishes that bail discretion must be exercised judiciously, considering the heinous nature of the crime, severity of punishment, and prima facie evidence.

rules.case_name: Prahlad Singh Bhati v. NCT, Delhi and Another
rules.reference: Prahlad Singh Bhati v. NCT, Delhi and Another
rules.relevance: Cited for factors to consider in bail, including nature of accusations, severity of punishment, and apprehension of witness tampering.

rules.case_name: Prasanta Kumar Sarkar v. Ashis Chatterjee and another
rules.reference: Prasanta Kumar Sarkar v. Ashis Chatterjee and another
rules.relevance: Lists factors for bail consideration including prima facie grounds, gravity of accusation, danger of absconding, and character of the accused.

rules.case_name: Dr. Narendra K. Amin v. State of Gujarat and another
rules.reference: Dr. Narendra K. Amin v. State of Gujarat and another
rules.relevance: Holds that an order granting bail is vulnerable if irrelevant materials are considered or relevant factors are ignored, rendering it perverse.

rules.reference: Balance between Liberty and Social Security
rules.relevance: Individual liberty is not absolute and must be balanced against collective security and the rule of law, especially in cases involving heinous crimes.
Defines criminal conspiracy; requires proof of an agreement between parties to commit an unlawful act.
Renders confessions made by a person in police custody inadmissible against them, unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate.

rules.case_name: Indra Dalal v. State Of Haryana
rules.reference: Indra Dalal v. State Of Haryana
rules.relevance: Establishes that conviction based solely on confessional statements without corroborative evidence is unsafe.

rules.case_name: Uppa alias Manjunatha v. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: Uppa alias Manjunatha v. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: Holds that confirmation of sentence by the High Court requires sound reasons based on analysis of material evidence.
A High Court in revisional jurisdiction cannot go behind a final decree to re-examine settled issues of title or fact.
Revisional jurisdiction is limited to correcting jurisdictional errors and does not permit the admission of fresh evidence or re-adjudication of merits.
A decree cannot be defeated by technical or hyper-technical objections; the Executing Court must take independent steps to identify land using available records.
Defines the scope of an executing court's power to determine questions relating to the execution of a decree, specifically allowing objections if the decree is a nullity.

Governs procedure when a party fails to present a written statement; the court held this rule is permissive and does not mandate judgment if other defendants contest the suit or if jurisdiction is disputed.
The court analyzed the scope of the Executive Magistrate's jurisdiction, noting it is summary in nature, deals with possession to prevent breach of peace, and does not determine title.
Defines 'judgment' as the statement of grounds for a decree; the court held the 1991 order lacked the required reasoning to constitute a judgment.
Mandates that a judgment must contain a concise statement of the case, points for determination, and reasons for the decision.
Defines 'decree' as the formal expression of an adjudication; the court held that without a valid judgment/adjudication, no valid decree exists.

rules.case_name: Balraj Taneja v. Sunil Madan
rules.relevance: Established that courts should not pass mechanical judgments under Order VIII Rule 10 without ensuring facts are proved or admitted, and that reasons must be recorded.
Establishes the statutory requirement that a plaintiff must affirmatively show that they have been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract throughout the period of the suit.
Empowers the court to extend time for payment of purchase money or rescind the contract if the purchaser fails to pay within the allowed period.

rules.case_name: Ramrati Kuer Vs. Dwarika Prasad Singh
rules.reference: Ramrati Kuer Vs. Dwarika Prasad Singh
rules.relevance: Held that no adverse inference can be drawn from the non-production of accounts unless a specific prayer was made to the court to order their production and the party failed to comply.

rules.case_name: Indira Kaur and Ors. Vs. Sheo Lal Kapoor
rules.reference: Indira Kaur and Ors. Vs. Sheo Lal Kapoor
rules.relevance: Held that no adverse inference can be drawn against a plaintiff for not producing a passbook unless specifically called upon to do so by the defendant or the Court.

rules.case_name: Beemaneni Maha Lakshmi Vs. Gangumalla Appa Rao
rules.reference: Beemaneni Maha Lakshmi Vs. Gangumalla Appa Rao
rules.relevance: Held that failure to demonstrate having sufficient money by the date of evidence is not of much consequence if readiness and willingness are otherwise established through conduct and testimony.
Prescribes a five-year limitation period for filing suits for specific performance, serving as a benchmark for reasonable time in exercising discretion.
Specific performance is an equitable remedy; the court must consider all attendant circumstances, and he who seeks equity must do equity.

rules.case_name: Sardar Mohan Singh v. Mangilal
rules.relevance: Establishes that the court retains jurisdiction to extend time for compliance with a conditional decree for specific performance.

rules.case_name: Ramankutty Guptan v. Avara
rules.relevance: Holds that when the trial court and executing court are the same, the executing court can entertain applications for extension of time under Section 28.

rules.case_name: K.S. Vidyanadam & Ors. v. Vairavan
rules.relevance: Indicates that delay coupled with a rise in property prices can make specific performance inequitable.
Defines the offence of murder committed in furtherance of a common intention, for which the appellants were convicted.
Permits the court to allow the party calling a witness to put questions as if in cross-examination if the witness is hostile, without effacing the evidence from the record.

rules.case_name: Ram Babu v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Ram Babu v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that the Supreme Court ordinarily does not interfere with concurrent findings of fact by the trial court and High Court unless there is a perversity or legal error.

rules.case_name: Prithi v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Reiterates that the evidence of a hostile witness is not rejected in toto but can be relied upon to the extent it is dependable and corroborated.

rules.case_name: Khujji @ Surendra Tiwari v. State of MP
rules.reference: Khujji @ Surendra Tiwari v. State of MP
rules.relevance: Confirms that a witness's evidence remains admissible even if declared hostile, provided it is corroborated by other reliable evidence.
Defines the offence of murder for which Accused Nos. 1 to 3 were convicted.
Defines the gravity of the offences, including murder and rioting, which is a primary factor in bail considerations.
Used to establish the serious criminal antecedents of Kunwar Singh and Rafal Singh.
Used to establish the serious criminal antecedents of Kunwar Singh.

rules.reference: Bail Jurisprudence: Criminal Antecedents and Witness Tampering
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that bail may be cancelled or denied if the accused has a history of criminal activity that suggests a likelihood of tampering with evidence or intimidating witnesses.
The substantive law under which the appellant was charged and convicted for murder.
The court applied the principle that the benefit of reasonable doubt must be given to the accused when doubts emerge from the evidence on record.

rules.reference: Reliance on testimony of hostile witnesses
rules.relevance: The court considered the principle that testimony of witnesses who turn hostile can be relied upon if corroborated, but must be scrutinized with great caution.
The substantive law under which the appellant was convicted for murder.
Defines the offence of causing disappearance of evidence, part of the conviction.
Defines the authority of magistrates to record confessions; requires Second Class Magistrates to be specially empowered by the State Government.
Governs the examination of the accused; the court noted the appellant's failure to explain circumstances appearing against her.

rules.case_name: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Singhara Singh and Others
rules.reference: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Singhara Singh and Others
rules.relevance: Held that a confession recorded by a Second Class Magistrate not specially empowered during investigation is inadmissible, and oral evidence of such confession is also barred.
The court applied the principle that in circumstantial cases, the chain of evidence must be complete, unbroken, and incapable of explanation on any hypothesis other than the guilt of the accused.

rules.case_name: H. N. Rishbud and Inder Singh v. The State of Delhi
rules.reference: H. N. Rishbud and Inder Singh v. The State of Delhi
rules.relevance: Established that the discovery and arrest of a suspected offender are essential steps in the course of an investigation.
The statutory basis for claiming compensation for death or injury in motor accidents.
The court established that the purpose of compensation is to fully and adequately restore the aggrieved party to the position prior to the accident.

rules.case_name: Yadav Kumar v. The Divisional Manager, National Insurance Company Ltd.
rules.reference: Yadav Kumar v. The Divisional Manager, National Insurance Company Ltd.
rules.relevance: Defined 'just compensation' as requiring fair, equitable principles and a reasonable approach, not merely a mathematical calculation.

rules.case_name: Sarla Verma and Ors. v. Delhi Transport Corporation and Ors.
rules.reference: Sarla Verma and Ors. v. Delhi Transport Corporation and Ors.
rules.relevance: Provided the multiplier table; the court applied a multiplier of 17 for a 29-year-old claimant.

rules.case_name: Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar
rules.relevance: Established that loss of future earnings must be assessed based on the impact of permanent disability on earning capacity.

rules.case_name: Puttamma and Ors. v. K.L. Narayana Reddy and Anr.
rules.reference: Puttamma and Ors. v. K.L. Narayana Reddy and Anr.
rules.relevance: Supported the enhancement of compensation for special diet and nutrition due to inflation and increased cost of living.
Mandates the grant of 'just compensation', which must be fair, equitable, and reasonable, neither a bonanza nor a pittance.

rules.case_name: Ramesh Chandra v. Randhir Singh
rules.relevance: Established that compensation for loss of earning capacity is distinct from and does not overlap with compensation for pain, suffering, and loss of enjoyment of life.

rules.reference: Distinction between Pecuniary and Non-Pecuniary Damages
rules.relevance: Pecuniary damages cover financial losses like loss of earnings, while non-pecuniary damages cover pain, suffering, and loss of amenities; these are distinct heads of claim.

rules.case_name: B. Kothandapani v. Tamil Nadu State Transport Corporation Ltd.
rules.reference: B. Kothandapani v. Tamil Nadu State Transport Corporation Ltd.
rules.relevance: Reaffirmed that compensation for permanent disability is permissible even if loss of earning capacity is awarded, distinguishing between pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages.
Establishes constructive liability for every member of an unlawful assembly for offences committed in furtherance of the common object.
Defines unlawful assembly and the concept of common object.

rules.case_name: Lalji Vs. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Held that Section 149 creates vicarious liability and that it is not necessary for every member to perform an overt act if they share the common object.

rules.case_name: Yunis Vs. State of M.P.
rules.relevance: Confirmed that presence in an unlawful assembly is sufficient for conviction under Section 149 even if no specific overt act is imputed to the accused.

rules.case_name: Subal Ghorai Vs. State of WB.
rules.reference: Subal Ghorai Vs. State of WB.
rules.relevance: Reinforced that members sharing a common object are liable for offences committed by the assembly even without personal overt acts.

rules.case_name: State of Rajasthan Vs. Shiv Charan
rules.reference: State of Rajasthan Vs. Shiv Charan
rules.relevance: Clarified that common object can be formed on the spur of the moment and does not require prior concert.
Prescribes punishment for murder; the court determined if the common object to beat included knowledge that death was a likely consequence.
The court relied on Section 34 to uphold constructive liability for the appellants despite the acquittal of other accused persons.
The court imposed a sentence for being a member of an unlawful assembly under this section.

The court held that an appellate court is untrammelled in re-evaluating evidence but must exercise restraint when overturning an acquittal; it cannot overturn merely because a different view is possible, but may do so if the trial court's finding is perverse or ignores credible corroboration.
Referenced in the context of the High Court's earlier declaration that the amending Act was ultra vires due to violation of Article 14.

rules.reference: M.P. Ashaskiya Shikshan Sanstha (Adhyapakon Tatha Anya Karamchariyaon Ke Vetano Ka Sandaya) Adhiniyam, 1978
rules.relevance: The statute governs the payment of salaries and grants-in-aid to teachers in aided institutions, the validity of which is central to the dispute.
Referenced in the context of the High Court's earlier declaration that the amending Act was ultra vires due to violation of Article 21.

rules.case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. Vs. Sharique Ali & Ors.
rules.reference: State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. Vs. Sharique Ali & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on the orders in this matter, specifically the direction to pay 50% grant-in-aid and the stay on the High Court's judgment declaring the Adhiniyam invalid, to frame the interim relief.

rules.reference: Contempt jurisdiction limited to non-compliance of clear orders
rules.relevance: The court considered whether directions could be issued in contempt proceedings when the underlying substantive issue (validity of the Act) was still pending before the Supreme Court.
Recognized as an equitable principle, but the court held it does not empower the High Court to usurp the constitutional function of the Chief Justice to fix pay scales under Article 229(2).

rules.reference: Article 309 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The court considered this provision as the source of power for the State Government to frame the Revision of Pay and Allowances Rules (ROPA), which are binding statutory rules.

rules.reference: Revision of Pay and Allowances Rules (ROPA Rules)
rules.relevance: The court held that the State is bound by these statutory rules fixing pay scales and cannot be compelled to act contrary to them.

rules.reference: Article 323-A of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The court relied on this article to establish that the jurisdiction of Administrative Tribunals is conferred by the Constitution and cannot be delegated to executive authorities.
The court cited these sections to define the exclusive jurisdiction and powers of Administrative Tribunals to adjudicate service disputes, noting they cannot delegate this duty.
Defines the offence of rape, which was the primary charge against the accused.
Defines the offence of outraging the modesty of a woman, an additional charge against the accused.

rules.case_name: State of Rajasthan v. Om Prakash
rules.reference: State of Rajasthan v. Om Prakash
rules.relevance: Establishes that conviction under Section 376 IPC can be based on the sole testimony of a rape victim if it is credible and convincing.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Gurmit Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Gurmit Singh
rules.relevance: Holds that a victim of sexual assault is not an accomplice and her evidence should not be viewed with suspicion; seeking corroboration as a rule adds insult to injury.

rules.case_name: Panchhi v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Establishes that evidence of a child witness cannot be rejected outrightly but must be evaluated with greater circumspection to ensure it is voluntary and free from tutoring.
Defines the offence of rape under which the appellant was convicted.

rules.case_name: Mohd. Kalam v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Mohd. Kalam v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Reiterates that evidence of a child cannot be rejected outrightly and must be evaluated with great circumspection.
Defines the offence of rape committed against a minor girl, under which the respondent was convicted.
Defines the offence of criminal intimidation, under which the respondent was convicted for threatening the prosecutrix.

rules.case_name: Tulsidas Kanojia v. State of Gujarat
rules.reference: Tulsidas Kanojia v. State of Gujarat
rules.relevance: Establishes that delay in lodging an FIR is not a mitigating circumstance if satisfactorily explained, particularly when the victim is unaware of the catastrophe.
The court applied this section to determine that a transfer during the pendency of a suit is not void but is subject to the rights of the parties as determined by the decree in that suit.

rules.case_name: Jayaram Mudaliar v. Ayyaswami
rules.relevance: Established that the purpose of Section 52 is not to defeat just and equitable claims but to subject them to the authority of the court dealing with the property.

rules.case_name: Hardev Singh v. Gurmail Singh
rules.relevance: Established that Section 52 does not declare a pendente lite transfer void or illegal, but only makes the purchaser bound by the decision in the pending litigation.

This provision allows for the rejection of a plaint if the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law. The court analyzed the scope of this provision to determine if factual disputes could be adjudicated at this stage.

The court established that Order VII, Rule 11(d) has limited application and requires that the bar by law be apparent from the averments in the plaint alone, without considering external evidence or disputed questions of fact.

rules.case_name: Balasaria Construction (P) Ltd. v. Hanuman Seva Trust and Others
rules.reference: Balasaria Construction (P) Ltd. v. Hanuman Seva Trust and Others
rules.relevance: Held that a plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII, Rule 11(d) for issues like limitation or bar by law if they involve mixed questions of law and fact requiring evidence.

rules.case_name: Natrajan v. Ashim Bai & Anr
rules.relevance: Held that for rejection of plaint, only averments in the plaint are relevant and the court cannot consider the defense case or evidence at that stage.

rules.case_name: Liverpool & London S.P & I Association Ltd. v. M. V Sea Success I & Anr
rules.reference: Liverpool & London S.P & I Association Ltd. v. M. V Sea Success I & Anr
rules.relevance: Clarified that the purpose of Order VII, Rule 11 is to avoid protracting hearings for suits that disclose no cause of action, but the test is whether the averments in the plaint, taken as correct, disclose a cause of action.

rules.reference: Evidence cannot be led beyond pleadings
rules.relevance: The court applied this principle to hold that evidence regarding the 1965 partition could not be considered because the amendment application to plead it was rejected.
A coparcener has no right to sell his undivided share in joint family property, and any such sale does not bind the other coparceners.
Prescribes that appointment to selection grades must be made by selection on merit with due regard to seniority.

rules.case_name: Sant Ram Sharma v. State of Rajasthan
rules.reference: Sant Ram Sharma v. State of Rajasthan
rules.relevance: Established that promotion to selection posts is based primarily on merit, and seniority is relevant only when merit is equal.

rules.case_name: State of Mysore v. Syed Mahmood
rules.reference: State of Mysore v. Syed Mahmood
rules.relevance: Held that in seniority-cum-merit promotions, an officer cannot claim promotion as a matter of right by virtue of seniority alone.

rules.case_name: R.K. Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: R.K. Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Relied on by the appellant for backdating promotion; the court distinguished it by noting that eligibility is different from actual promotion and that merit comparison was pending.
Referenced regarding the practice of the Court not interfering with interlocutory orders under its special leave jurisdiction.
The court examined whether the High Level Committee adhered to the prescribed criteria and procedures under these rules when evaluating the appellant's fitness for promotion.
The court applied the principle that it will not interfere with the findings of a high-level committee if the claim was objectively considered and the process was compliant with rules.

rules.reference: Judicial restraint in evaluating relative merits
rules.relevance: The court recognized its inability to independently evaluate the relative merits of candidates for promotion, deferring to the specialized assessment of the competent authority.
Governs temporary appointment of non-cadre officers to cadre posts, requiring specific approvals and reports to the Central Government, which were not complied with in this case.

rules.reference: Indian Forest Service (Regulation of Seniority) Rules, 1968
rules.relevance: This rule governs the assignment of year of allotment for promoted officers. Explanation 1 mandates that the benefit of continuous officiation counts only from the later of the date of inclusion in the select list or the date of officiating appointment, implying both conditions must co-exist throughout the period.
Governs the power of the Committee of Chief Commissioners to review orders and direct the filing of appeals, including the three-month limitation period for issuing such directions.
Empowers the Appellate Tribunal to admit an appeal after the expiry of the relevant period if satisfied that there was sufficient cause for the delay.

Reduced the limitation period for the reviewing authority to three months, creating parity with the limitation period for assessees, which the Court used to interpret legislative intent regarding condonation of delay.

rules.case_name: Central Excise v. M.M. Rubber Co.
rules.reference: Central Excise v. M.M. Rubber Co.
rules.relevance: Held that orders passed beyond limitation are invalid; distinguished by the Supreme Court as applicable to the pre-2008 statutory scheme with a one-year limitation period, not the post-2008 scheme.

rules.case_name: CCE v. Monnet Ispat & Energy Ltd.
rules.reference: CCE v. Monnet Ispat & Energy Ltd.
rules.relevance: Full Bench decision holding that the Tribunal has ample power to condone delay in filing appeals under Section 35-E(4), including delay attributable to the reviewing committee.
The court examined the scope of the High Court's writ jurisdiction and whether it could be exercised despite the existence of an alternative statutory remedy.

rules.reference: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
rules.relevance: This section provides a specific statutory mechanism for appeals against orders passed by adjudicating authorities, which serves as the alternative remedy in this case.
The court applied the principle that the existence of an alternative remedy is not an absolute bar to writ jurisdiction but restricts it to exceptional circumstances.

The court identified specific exceptions where writ jurisdiction can be exercised despite an alternative remedy: breach of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, excess of jurisdiction, or challenge to the vires of the statute.
The court considered whether the procedural restrictions and limitation period under Section 11B applied to refund claims arising from provisional assessments.
The court distinguished between losing control of a firm and the inability to manage day-to-day functions due to age or health, holding that majority shareholding constitutes retaining control.

rules.reference: Liberal view for widows and physically handicapped
rules.relevance: The court held that the law should take a more liberal and humanitarian view in cases involving widows and physically handicapped persons, particularly regarding their source of livelihood.
Requires State instrumentalities to act fairly, reasonably, and without arbitrariness; used to strike down unconscionable contract terms.
Defines 'State' to include instrumentalities, making IOCL subject to fundamental rights scrutiny.
Establishes that acceptance must be absolute and unqualified; used to determine that the unexecuted standard agreement did not form a concluded contract.
Bars specific performance of determinable contracts; the court analyzed whether the distributorship agreement fell under this category.

rules.case_name: Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. v. Brojo Nath Ganguly
rules.reference: Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. v. Brojo Nath Ganguly
rules.relevance: Establishes that courts will not enforce unfair or unreasonable contracts or clauses where there is a significant disparity in bargaining power between parties.

rules.case_name: Mahabir Auto Stores v. Indian Oil Corporation
rules.reference: Mahabir Auto Stores v. Indian Oil Corporation
rules.relevance: Affirms that IOCL, as a State instrumentality, is bound by Article 14 to act reasonably and fairly in its contractual dealings.
An agreement not executed by the parties cannot be legally enforced against them.

This rule deals with the procedure in case of assignment or devolution of interest during the pendency of a suit, allowing the court to grant leave to prosecute the suit against the person upon whom the interest has devolved.

rules.reference: Error apparent on the face of the record
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court held that a judgment based on a factually incorrect premise (patient's death) constitutes an error apparent on the face of the record that goes to the root of the matter.

The court held that inherent powers cannot be used to correct a fundamental factual issue that forms the basis of the judgment, especially without notice to the affected party, as this amounts to altering the sanctity of the framed issues.
The provision under which the Appellants sought quashing of the complaint and summoning order in the High Court.

The Supreme Court's order dated 23.03.2020 was passed under Article 142. The court analyzed its scope to determine if it applied to police investigations.
This section requires production of an arrested person before a Magistrate within 24 hours, serving as a safeguard for personal liberty supplementary to Section 167.
Article 21 protects the right to life and personal liberty. The court held that this right cannot be curtailed by lockdown restrictions or the limitation order.
The provision under which the appellant filed the petition to quash the criminal proceedings.
The court distinguished the lockdown from a proclamation of Emergency under Article 352 to reject the argument that fundamental rights were suspended.

rules.case_name: Uday Mohanlal Acharya v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Uday Mohanlal Acharya v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Established that Section 167 is supplementary to Section 57 and that the right to bail after the expiry of the statutory period is compulsive.

rules.case_name: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Established the 'rarest of the rare' doctrine and the principle that death penalty should be awarded only when the alternative of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed.
A principle of circumstantial evidence where guilt is inferred if the victim is last seen with the accused and the time gap is not sufficient for the victim to have been with anyone else.
Defines the offence of murder and prescribes the punishment, including death or life imprisonment.
Defines unnatural offences, including pederasty, which was established in this case.
Requires the court to record special reasons for imposing the death sentence instead of life imprisonment.

rules.case_name: Shankar Kisanrao Khade v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Shankar Kisanrao Khade v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Laid down the 'crime test', 'criminal test', and 'RR test' (society-centric test) for determining the appropriateness of the death penalty.

Requires the court to record special reasons for imposing the death penalty instead of life imprisonment.
Mandates the recording of circumstances relating to the offence and the offender before sentencing.

rules.reference: Right to Fair Trial and Judicial Calm
rules.relevance: The court held that a hasty trial depriving the accused of adequate time to prepare a defense violates the principle of fair trial and judicial calm, necessitating a de novo trial.

This rule governs the amendment of pleadings. The court noted that while amendments are generally considered liberally, they cannot override specific statutory interdicts like Order VIII Rule 6A.

rules.case_name: Gurbachan Singh Vs. Bhag Singh and Ors.
rules.reference: Gurbachan Singh Vs. Bhag Singh and Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that a counter-claim or set-off must be pleaded in the written statement before the time limit for delivering it expires.

rules.case_name: Mahendra Kumar Vs. Staff of Madhya Pradesh
rules.reference: Mahendra Kumar Vs. Staff of Madhya Pradesh
rules.relevance: Held that belated counter-claims are impermissible.

rules.case_name: Shanti Rani Das: Dewanjee (Smt.) Vs. Dinesh Chandra Day (Dead) by Lrs.
rules.reference: Shanti Rani Das: Dewanjee (Smt.) Vs. Dinesh Chandra Day (Dead) by Lrs.
rules.relevance: Held that belated counter-claims are impermissible.

rules.case_name: H. N. Rishbud and Inder Singh v. The State of Delhi

The court noted that forgery of a record of a court or public register under this section is not covered by Section 195(1)(b) or (c) of the CrPC.

These provisions bar a Magistrate from taking cognizance of certain offences unless a complaint is made by the court before which the offence was committed or a subordinate court. The court analyzed whether the charged offences fell within this bar.

The court held that the offence of giving false information under this section is not covered by the jurisdictional bars of Section 195(1)(b) or (c) of the CrPC.

The court held that while using a forged document as genuine is covered by Section 195(1)(c), the bar only applies if the offence is committed by a 'party' to the proceedings.

The court acknowledged that accused persons are entitled to humane treatment and due medical care while in prison, but this does not automatically mandate bail if adequate care is provided within the prison system.

rules.reference: Duty to consider all materials on record

Detention beyond the legally permissible sentence violates the right to life and personal liberty.

rules.reference: Article 14 of the Constitution of India

rules.case_name: Haldiram Bhujiawala and Anr. v. Anand Kumar Deepak Kumar and Anr.

A saving clause listing specific enactments where the Act does not apply; the absence of IPC Section 397 from this list was key to the court's interpretation.

rules.case_name: Ramji Missar v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Ramji Missar v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Established that Section 6 of the Act applies based on the offender's age at the time of sentencing, not the commission of the offence.

rules.case_name: Ishar Das v. State of Punjab

rules.case_name: CCE v. Bahubali

rules.case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Vikram Das
rules.reference: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Vikram Das
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this judgment, which held that courts cannot impose less than the minimum sentence, by clarifying that the Probation of Offenders Act is not excluded by mandatory minimums under the IPC.

rules.case_name: Anwarul Haq v. State of U. P.

rules.case_name: Dharma Pal and Others v. State of Punjab

Defines the power of the High Court to appeal against an order of acquittal.

rules.case_name: Murugesan v. State Through Inspector of Police

rules.relevance: Establishes the broad principles governing the appellate court's power to review evidence in acquittal appeals.

rules.case_name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
rules.reference: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
rules.relevance: The court relied on this judgment to confirm that reserved category candidates selected on merit are not counted against the reserved quota and are treated as open competition candidates.

The court used these clauses to confirm that candidates not availing relaxation are treated as general category and cannot claim reserved vacancies unless it improves service choice.

Statements recorded under this section have evidentiary value and were used to establish the appellant's complicity in the conspiracy.
This section creates a presumption that property involved is proceeds of crime, shifting the burden of proof to the accused to demonstrate that the property is not proceeds of crime.
Defines 'proceeds of crime' as property derived or obtained as a result of criminal activity relating to a scheduled offence.

rules.case_name: Gautam Kundu Vs. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.reference: Gautam Kundu Vs. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.relevance: Established that Section 45 of the PMLA has an overriding effect on the Code of Criminal Procedure and imposes mandatory conditions for bail that must be strictly complied with.

rules.case_name: Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank

rules.relevance: Established that the Adjudicating Authority's role under Section 7 is limited to ascertaining the existence of default and does not extend to deciding merits or directing settlements.

Preserves the inherent powers of the Tribunal to make orders necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of process.

rules.case_name: Charan Lal Sahu v. Union of India
rules.reference: Charan Lal Sahu v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Elucidates the Doctrine of Necessity, allowing an adjudicator to act if no other competent tribunal can be constituted.

rules.case_name: Election Commission of India v. Dr. Subramaniam Swamy
rules.reference: Election Commission of India v. Dr. Subramaniam Swamy
rules.relevance: Clarifies that the Doctrine of Necessity permits an authority to decide issues when no other judge or authority is available to prevent a stalemate.
This section governs the registration of trusts for tax exemption. The court considered whether the Trust's conduct warranted cancellation of this registration due to misuse.
This section provides deductions for donations. The court considered the cancellation of this approval as it was being misused alongside Section 12AA.

rules.reference: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
rules.relevance: Defines the offence of disclosing the identity of a child victim, punishable with imprisonment up to one year.

rules.reference: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
rules.relevance: Contains a non-obstante clause regarding the reporting of offences; central to the dispute over whether it overrides Cr.P.C. investigation procedures.
Mandates that no police officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate.
Provides that offences under other laws are investigated according to Cr.P.C. provisions, subject to any enactment regulating the manner of investigation.
Saving clause stating that Cr.P.C. does not affect special laws in the absence of a specific provision to the contrary.

rules.case_name: Keshav Lal Thakur v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Keshav Lal Thakur v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Held that investigation of a non-cognizable offence without Magistrate's order under Section 155(2) is illegal and vitiates subsequent proceedings.

rules.case_name: Fertico Marketing and Investment Private Limited v. Central Bureau of Investigation
rules.reference: Fertico Marketing and Investment Private Limited v. Central Bureau of Investigation
rules.relevance: Held that illegality in investigation does not vitiate cognizance or trial unless it causes a miscarriage of justice.

rules.case_name: H.N. Rishbud v. State of Delhi
rules.reference: H.N. Rishbud v. State of Delhi
rules.relevance: Established that invalidity of investigation does not necessarily nullify cognizance unless it affects the competence of the court or causes miscarriage of justice.

rules.reference: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
rules.relevance: Defines the offence of aggravated penetrative sexual assault, which requires proof of assault.
Section 386(b)(iii) prohibits enhancing a sentence in an appeal from conviction unless the accused is given an opportunity to show cause. The proviso explicitly mandates notice before enhancement.
Defines the limited grounds for setting aside an award, including misconduct, invalid proceedings, or the award being improperly procured or otherwise invalid.

rules.case_name: Champsey Bhara & Co. v. Jivraj Balloo Spg. & F Wvg Co. Ltd.
rules.reference: Champsey Bhara & Co. v. Jivraj Balloo Spg. & F Wvg Co. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Establishes that courts have no jurisdiction to investigate the merits of the case or examine evidence to determine if an arbitrator committed an error of law.

rules.case_name: Arosan Enterprises Ltd. v. Union of India and Anr.
rules.reference: Arosan Enterprises Ltd. v. Union of India and Anr.
rules.relevance: Holds that re-appraisal of evidence by the Court is not permissible in proceedings under Section 30 of the Arbitration Act.

rules.case_name: Jivraj Bhai U.S. and others v. Chintaman Rao Balaji & Ors.
rules.reference: Jivraj Bhai U.S. and others v. Chintaman Rao Balaji & Ors.
rules.relevance: Establishes that it is not open to the court to speculate on the mental process of an Arbitrator where no reasons are given in the award.

rules.case_name: Ralliaram Union of India v. A.I. Ralliaram
rules.reference: Ralliaram Union of India v. A.I. Ralliaram
rules.relevance: States that an arbitrator's decision is binding right or wrong, except in cases of error of law on the face of the award.

rules.case_name: State of Andhra Pradesh and Ors. v. R. V. Rayamin & Ors.
rules.reference: State of Andhra Pradesh and Ors. v. R. V. Rayamin & Ors.
rules.relevance: Distinguished because it applies to speaking awards where reasoning can be examined, unlike the non-speaking award in the present case.

rules.case_name: V.G. George v. Indian Rare Earths Ltd. & Anr.
rules.reference: V.G. George v. Indian Rare Earths Ltd. & Anr.
rules.relevance: Distinguished because it concerned misconduct under Section 30(a) and involved a speaking award, whereas the present case concerns Section 30(c) and a non-speaking award.

rules.case_name: Associated Engineering Co. v. Government of Andhra Pradesh & Anr.
rules.reference: Associated Engineering Co. v. Government of Andhra Pradesh & Anr.
rules.relevance: Distinguished because it involved an arbitrator who acted beyond the scope of the contract, whereas there is no evidence here that the Umpire exceeded jurisdiction.
The court held that Section 34 provides an exhaustive list of grounds for setting aside an award, and non-stamping or non-registration is not among them.
Vests the power to enlarge time in the Court and declares void any provision in an agreement allowing the arbitrator to enlarge time except with the consent of all parties.

rules.reference: Madhya Pradesh Entertainment Duty and Advertisements Tax Act, 1936
rules.relevance: The court interpreted these provisions to determine if DTH broadcasting constituted 'admission to an entertainment' in a specified place, concluding it did not.

rules.reference: Madhya Pradesh Entertainment Duty and Advertisements Tax Rules, 1942
rules.relevance: The court examined the rules to confirm that the collection machinery relied on revenue stamps for tickets, which is inapplicable to DTH.
The court considered the challenge regarding equality, specifically the distinction between taxing cable operators and not taxing Doordarshan.
The court applied the principle that if the collection machinery provided under a taxing statute cannot be applied to an event, the event is beyond the charge created by the statute.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Income Tax v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty
rules.reference: Commissioner of Income Tax v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty
rules.relevance: Cited to support the principle that if the collection machinery is inapplicable, the event is outside the taxing net.
The court held that the notification dated May 5, 2008, could not enlarge the charging section or amend the collection provisions of the Act.
The court examined the definitions of 'cable television', 'television exhibition', and 'entertainment' and the charging section to determine the scope and validity of the tax.
The court analyzed whether the tax violated the freedom of speech and expression and the right to carry on business, concluding that business aspects intertwined with speech can be taxed.

rules.case_name: Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Government of India & Others v. Cricket Association of Bengal & Others
rules.reference: Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Government of India & Others v. Cricket Association of Bengal & Others
rules.relevance: The court relied on the principle that where speech and conduct are joined in a single course of action, free speech values must be balanced against competing societal interests.

rules.case_name: Express Newspapers v. Union of India
rules.reference: Express Newspapers v. Union of India
rules.relevance: The court used this precedent to establish that while there can be no tax on the right to exercise freedom of expression, tax is leviable on the profession, occupation, trade, business, and industry aspect of the press or similar entities.
